name: Star of India
label: Star of India
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'North Harbor Drive' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of North Harbor Drive nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/170659470: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Star of India' (66 m across).
notes: 1863 tall ship at the Maritime Museum of San Diego.

text.description: Star of India is a tall, three-masted sailing ship moored on the San Diego waterfront. She was built in 1863 on the Isle of Man as a ship called Euterpe, and her iron hull has survived almost unchanged since then. She is now part of the Maritime Museum of San Diego and is said to be the oldest ship in the world that still sails regularly. That history helps the photos: the dark hull, the tall masts and the rigging make strong shapes against the sky, and the bay and Embarcadero behind her show where she sits. The ship is long, and you can't fit all of her in from most places on land. The best full-length view is from the sidewalk on North Harbor Drive, where the hull and all three masts fit in one frame. Stand and the ship lies to the west. From there, keep the masts upright and leave a little sky above the top of them. Once you have the full view, walk closer for details such as the bow figurehead, the captain's wheel and the rigging against the other museum masts. If you are still here at sunset, the Embarcadero is a good second spot. The light on the water, the ship in the foreground and the lights of Point Loma in the distance make a different kind of picture.
text.geographic_location: On the San Diego waterfront, just west of downtown and just south of San Diego International Airport. The ship is moored on the west side of North Harbor Drive, roughly at Ash Street, with the other Maritime Museum ships to her north.
text.directions_text: From downtown San Diego, head to North Harbor Drive near Ash Street (on foot or however suits you) and walk to the waterfront sidewalk facing the ship. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full hull and three masts from the sidewalk. If you can't get far enough back, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the ship in the middle of the frame so the masts don't lean. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the figurehead, the captain's wheel and the rigging.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on North Harbor Drive (landside sidewalk facing the ship, morning light). The full hull and three masts of the Star of India with the Embarcadero and harbor behind it. The ship is to the west of you. From here the full hull and all three masts fit in one picture, with the Embarcadero and the harbour behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the masts up with the vertical lines. Put the hull along the lower third and leave sky above the tallest mast. For a different picture, walk closer and use the telephoto to fill the frame with the bow figurehead, the wheel or the rigging against the museum's other masts. At the Embarcadero, put the ship in the foreground with the bay and the lights of Point Loma behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the ship's hull to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the dark hull doesn't wash out. For the sunset shot at the Embarcadero, try night mode if the light fades, and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when it is sunny, is the time one guide recommends for shooting from the landside. Sunset suits the Embarcadero view, with the ship in the foreground and the bay lit behind it.

text.access_note: The ship belongs to the Maritime Museum of San Diego, so going aboard needs a museum ticket (check the official site before you go); the waterfront sidewalk view is free.
claims_not_in_sources: In the morning the sun is in the east, behind a photographer standing on the landside sidewalk, so it should light the ship from the front.
The North Harbor Drive sidewalk is a public pavement that anyone can walk along without a ticket.
It takes about 2 minutes on foot to cover the 93 m from the stand-here point to the ship (distance x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
The sunset view at the Embarcadero has the ship in the foreground, as the researched viewpoint notes describe.

name: San Diego Zoo
label: San Diego Zoo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Skyfari' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Alaska Airlines Skyfari' (way/79135682): point nearest the subject (532 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31274621: large area 'San Diego Zoo' (1207 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
San Diego Zoo sits inside Balboa Park and grew out of animals left over from the 1915 Panama–California Exposition. Today it covers about 100 acres and is home to more than 12,000 animals of over 680 species and subspecies. It was a pioneer of open-air, cage-less exhibits, so many enclosures use moats and planting instead of bars. That is good news for phone photographers, because you often get a clear view of an animal with greenery all around it.

The best way to take in the whole place is from the Skyfari, the open-air aerial tram. It was built in 1969 and carries you over the zoo at treetop level. From up there you see the planted habitats and animals below, with the rest of Balboa Park beyond and, on a clear day, sometimes the downtown skyline far off. Pictures from the ground tend to be close-ups of single animals. The Skyfari gives you the big picture of how the zoo is laid out among the trees.

Take a few frames at different moments of the ride, because the view changes as the tram moves. Keep your phone held steadily, and keep your arms and the phone inside the tram. Use the ultra-wide lens for the sweep of the landscape and the telephoto for animals and details below. Check the official site before you go for admission and Skyfari details.
text.geographic_location: The zoo is in Balboa Park, in San Diego, California. The Skyfari's east terminal is on the eastern side of the zoo grounds.
text.directions_text: Check local options for reaching Balboa Park and the zoo. Once inside, follow the signs to the Skyfari east terminal. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of treetops and habitats, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out animals or the park beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (East terminal (boarding from the east station, then the tram crosses the zoo)). A treetop-level aerial view over the zoo's planted habitats and animals, with Balboa Park beyond and sometimes the downtown skyline in the distance. Go into the zoo and board the Skyfari at the east terminal, where the viewpoint is. The tram then crosses the zoo. From the tram you look down on the zoo's planted habitats and animals, with Balboa Park beyond and sometimes the downtown skyline in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the canopy and habitats fill most of the frame. Include a few treetops in the foreground to give a sense of height. Take several frames as you travel, because the view keeps changing.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the middle distance and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks too bright. Live Photos or burst can help you catch a sharp frame while the tram moves. Use the ultra-wide lens only when you want a very broad view, as it makes distant things look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day for the view across Balboa Park and towards downtown. Mornings and late afternoons usually give softer light than midday.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed site, and the Skyfari needs zoo admission, so check the official site before you go for admission, Skyfari opening times and any closures.

name: Hotel del Coronado
label: Hotel del Coronado
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Coronado Beach' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Coronado Beach' (way/233833244): edge nearest the subject (2126 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1520316794: large area 'Hotel Del Coronado' (757 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Victorian beachfront resort hotel with red turrets.

text.description:
The Hotel del Coronado, often just called The Del, is a big white wooden Victorian seaside hotel with red turrets and a steep, busy roofline. It opened in 1888, when it was the largest resort hotel in the world. It is also a National Historic Landmark and is described as the second-largest wooden building in the United States. That mix of age, size and colour is why it photographs so well. The red roofs stand out against the sky, and the pale walls pick up the evening light.

The best-known view is from the public sand of Coronado Beach. From there the turrets and roofline rise over the dunes and ice plant, set against the sky. If you stand close, the whole building may not fit in the default lens (1x). Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width, or step back along the beach. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x) to pick out a single turret or the roof details. Keep any horizon level with the gridlines.

As a second choice, Orange Avenue gives you the entrance sign with the turrets behind it, but palm trees can hide the towers. Ocean Boulevard shows the hotel only in the distance, beyond the rock seawall. Take your photos from the beach or the public streets, and do not set up inside the hotel grounds.
text.geographic_location: The hotel is in Coronado, just across San Diego Bay from downtown San Diego. It sits right on the ocean beach, and the public sand next to it is where the classic photo is taken.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head to the Hotel del Coronado in Coronado. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full width of the building, then use the default lens (1x) for a natural view. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x) for a close-up of the turrets and roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (public sand just past the Hot Coal Bins line, shooting north-west toward the building). The red turrets and Victorian roofline rising over the dunes and ice plant, with the ocean and sky filling the lower frame. From there you see the red turrets and Victorian roofline rising over the dunes and ice plant.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the turrets in the upper-right or upper-left part of the frame. If the sea or horizon is in view, keep it level with a gridline. Include some dune grass in the foreground to give depth. For another view, try Orange Avenue for the entrance sign with the turrets behind it, or Ocean Boulevard for the hotel in the distance beyond the seawall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the roofs do not look washed out. In a wide scene, panorama mode can capture the whole frontage, but hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon and sunset, when the light hits the ocean side of the hotel and turns the white siding pink.

text.access_note: The beach is public and open for personal photos, but the hotel grounds are private and have photography restrictions, so check the official site before you go.

name: Petco Park
label: Petco Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Harbor Drive Pedestrian Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Harbor Drive Pedestrian Bridge' (way/1482288976): middle (163 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24616919: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Petco Park' (358 m across).

text.description: Petco Park is the home of the San Diego Padres baseball team, and it sits right at the edge of downtown, next to the Gaslamp Quarter. It opened in 2004. What makes it a good photo subject is the mix of old and new: a historic brick warehouse, the Western Metal Supply Co. building, was built into the ballpark, and its corner now serves as the left field foul pole. From the Harbor Drive Pedestrian Bridge you look across the trolley tracks to the stadium with the downtown buildings behind it. It is a good place for one wide, tidy shot that shows how the ballpark fits into the city. The walkway links the stadium to the Gaslamp Quarter, and trains pass beneath it, so you can wait for one to slide through the bottom of your frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens to take in the stadium, tracks and skyline together, and keep the phone level so the buildings stay straight. If you want a closer look at the red-brick warehouse, try the Western Metal Supply Co. Building from the street outside the ballpark. Park at the Park gives a higher, quieter view across the ballpark, but access there can change on game days, so check before you go. Expect more people on the bridge around game times.
text.geographic_location: Petco Park is in the East Village neighbourhood of downtown San Diego, next to the Gaslamp Quarter and across Harbor Drive from the San Diego Convention Center.
text.directions_text: Head for the Gaslamp Quarter or East Village in downtown San Diego and walk towards Harbor Drive, where the San Diego Trolley light rail runs along the ballpark's southern side. If you are coming by train, Santa Fe Depot is about a mile (1.6 km) from the ballpark. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the stadium, the trolley tracks and the skyline into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view with less distortion at the edges. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the brick warehouse or a train passing below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Harbor Drive Pedestrian Bridge. Stadium and downtown skyline seen from the walkway over the trolley tracks, with trains passing below. Face north: the stadium is ahead of you and the downtown skyline rises behind it, with trains passing underneath.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge rail or the tracks up with a horizontal line so the picture looks straight. Let the tracks lead the eye towards the stadium. Wait for a train to enter the bottom of the frame for some movement. If the bridge is busy or you want a different angle, try the Western Metal Supply Co. Building from outside the ballpark, or Park at the Park for a higher view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stadium to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the brick and the buildings keep their colour. Try a Live Photo or a short burst to catch a train at the right moment. Hold the phone steady against the rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Facing north, the sun is mostly behind you or to one side for much of the day, so the stadium front should be well lit. Early morning is likely to be quieter. Around dusk, night mode can help with the lights, but rest your elbows on the rail to keep the shot sharp.

text.access_note: The bridge is a public walkway, but access to the ballpark itself and to viewing areas such as Park at the Park can change on game days, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Facing north from the bridge, the sun is behind or beside you for much of the day, so the stadium front should be well lit.
Early morning is likely to be quieter on the bridge.
The bridge is likely to be busier around game times.
Trains pass under the bridge regularly enough to wait for one.

name: Balboa Park
label: Balboa Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Botanical Building' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Botanical Building' (way/25775425): middle (78 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15082953: large area 'Balboa Park' (3664 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic cultural park with Spanish Colonial Revival architecture and gardens.

text.description:
Balboa Park is a big, green cultural park next to Downtown San Diego, and its most photographed scene is the Botanical Building seen across the Lily Pond. The pond lies in front of the building, with the lush greenery and ornate facade behind it, so you get a calm foreground, a strong subject and plenty of sky. The pond also gives you a reflection to include. Several photo guides name this as the park's most-photographed view, and it suits both portraits and quick snapshots.

The park covers about 1,200 acres and has been set aside for public recreation since 1835. It hosted two major expositions, in 1915-16 and 1935-36, and the Spanish Colonial Revival buildings along the El Prado promenade date from that tradition. The Botanical Building was designed by Carleton Winslow for the 1915 exposition. It was then the largest wood lath structure in the world. The park and its historic exposition buildings became a National Historic Landmark District in 1977.

For your photo, stand at the water's edge and keep the building centred, so both sides of the facade look balanced. If you have time, two other views are worth a look. One is Plaza de Panama, looking along the El Prado axis toward the California Tower. The other is Cabrillo Bridge, with the skyline in the distance. Weekends and holidays can be busy, so go early if you want the pond to yourself.
text.geographic_location: In the Central Mesa of Balboa Park, on the El Prado promenade, inside the park beyond the Cabrillo Bridge main entrance. The park is bordered by Downtown San Diego, Bankers Hill and North Park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Start from Downtown San Diego and head to the Cabrillo Bridge entrance. This is the park's main entrance, and it leads through the California Quadrangle onto El Prado. Then walk east along El Prado until you reach the Lily Pond and the Botanical Building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view of the pond, the building and its reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pond edge feels tight or the crowd is in the way. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the facade and the plants.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Botanical Building (in front of the building, across the Lily Pond). The reflecting Lily Pond in the foreground, with the Botanical Building's lush greenery and ornate facade behind it. From here the pond fills the foreground, and the building's lush greenery and ornate facade sit behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building on the centre line, with the pond taking the lower third of the frame. Crouch slightly to bring more of the water, and its reflection, into the shot. If you want a different view, try Plaza de Panama or Cabrillo Bridge as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the bright water keep their detail. Use portrait mode for people standing in front of the pond. Wait for ripples to settle before you take the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or sunset, according to one photo guide, when reflections on the water can look good. Check the light on the day.

text.access_note: The park is an open public space, but the Botanical Building's interior has been closed at times and some attractions, such as the Museum of Us tower tour, are paid, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing low at the water's edge helps include more of the reflection in the frame.
Ripples on the pond can spoil the reflection, so waiting for the water to settle helps.
Lowering the exposure slider can protect sky and bright-water detail in this scene.

name: USS Midway Museum
label: USS Midway Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tuna Harbor Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Tuna Harbor Park' (way/44500721): middle (312 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3329805: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Retired aircraft carrier turned museum on the Embarcadero.

text.description: The USS Midway Museum is a real aircraft carrier, moored at Navy Pier on San Diego Bay and open as a museum. Midway was the longest-serving US aircraft carrier of the 20th century, in service from 1945 to 1992, and it opened to visitors on 7 June 2004. Its long grey hull, the aircraft parked on deck and the downtown skyline behind it make a strong waterfront picture. One of the best spots recommended for a side view is Tuna Harbor Park, just south of the carrier. From there you can see the ship side-on, with the city behind, though views of the full ship from land can be limited. The Unconditional Surrender statue in the park gives you a foreground subject, which helps the huge ship look its size. Two alternatives are worth knowing. Broadway Pier gives the front and side of the carrier across the water, which suits low angles. Embarcadero Marina Park North gives a wider scene with the ship, a bridge, moored boats and the skyline. If you go aboard, you will find climb-aboard aircraft and cockpits, and scenes from Top Gun: Maverick were filmed here in 2018 and 2019. Allow a few minutes at your chosen viewpoint, and take one wide shot and one closer shot of the deck.
text.geographic_location: On Navy Pier, on the downtown San Diego waterfront along the Embarcadero, beside San Diego Bay. Tuna Harbor Park lies just to the south of the ship.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from downtown San Diego and head for the Embarcadero waterfront. From there the carrier is to the north, about 2 minutes on foot to the ship's pier. Check for any closures around the Embarcadero before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the side-on view from where you stand. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the ship will not fit, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out aircraft and details on the flight deck.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Tuna Harbor Park (south of the carrier, looking at the ship's broadside). The full length of the carrier seen side-on against the downtown skyline, with the Unconditional Surrender statue in the foreground. The carrier is to the north of you, and you are looking at its broadside against the downtown skyline. Place the Unconditional Surrender statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level so the long hull sits straight across the frame. Put the statue low in the frame, with the ship and skyline behind it. If you want an alternative, Broadway Pier gives a low-angle view of the front and side, and Embarcadero Marina Park North gives a wider scene with the bridge and boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the grey hull to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the ship does not look washed out. For the whole ship in one go, try panorama and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light on the ship's side is clean.

text.access_note: The waterfront around the ship is public space, but going aboard the museum is a ticketed visit, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tuna Harbor Park is south of the carrier and is one of the recommended spots for a side-on view with the downtown skyline behind; views of the full ship from land can be limited.
Early-morning light on the ship's side is clean (from Tuna Harbor Park).
The ship may not fit in the default lens (1x) frame from close range, so ultra-wide may be needed.
Tapping on the grey hull and lowering exposure helps keep the sky from washing out.
Going aboard the museum is ticketed; the surrounding waterfront is public.

name: Gaslamp Quarter
label: Gaslamp Quarter
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Balboa Theatre' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Balboa Theatre' (way/31843132): middle (55 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14393230: large area 'Gaslamp Quarter' (1044 m across): the middle of the area.
notes: Historic downtown entertainment district with its neon gateway arch.

text.description:
The Gaslamp Quarter is downtown San Diego's old Victorian district, and it is one of the easiest places in the city to photograph with a phone. Most of the area's 90-odd historic buildings date from the Victorian era. Today they hold restaurants, shops and bars, so the street fronts are colourful and full of detail. Alonzo Horton began developing this part of town in 1867 and chose Fifth Avenue as its main street. The district was later renamed 'Gaslamp Quarter' during the 1980s restoration, and the arched sign over Fifth Avenue went up in 1992.

Its Moorish and Spanish-style facade makes a calmer picture than the busy Fifth Avenue strip, and a visitor guide notes it is among the most photographed buildings in the district. Cross over so the whole front fits in, and keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. If you want the classic postcard view, walk on to the Gaslamp Quarter Archway, which frames the Victorian shopfronts along Fifth Avenue. Market Street is another good choice, with the old Louis Bank of Commerce building and the street lamps. Early morning is quieter, so you get cleaner shots with fewer people in the frame.
text.geographic_location: The Gaslamp Quarter is in downtown San Diego, running from Broadway down to Harbor Drive and from 4th to 6th Avenue. Petco Park is one block away, in the East Village.
text.directions_text: No Underground-style stops are listed for this spot, so start from the centre of downtown San Diego and head for the Balboa Theatre, either on foot or by taxi or hired scooter. Follow the main street grid south and look for the arched sign over Fifth Avenue. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole theatre front in from across the street. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and try telephoto (2x or more) for details on the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Balboa Theatre (Stand on the sidewalk across from the front facade). The theatre's Moorish and Spanish-style facade as a quieter architectural subject away from the main Fifth Avenue crowd. From there the whole Moorish and Spanish-style facade is in view, away from the main Fifth Avenue crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them. Keep the phone upright, not tilted back, so the facade does not lean. Then walk to the Gaslamp Quarter Archway for the Fifth Avenue postcard view, with the arched sign framing the Victorian fronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the detail. Use the ultra-wide sparingly, as it can stretch things near the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is quieter. For Market Street, warm low sun lights the old bank building nicely. In the evening the streets are busy and the signs and lamps are lit, so try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.

text.access_note: The streets and sidewalks are open public space, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside the theatre or any other building.

name: Old Town San Diego State Historic Park
label: Old Town State Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Casa de Estudillo' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'La Casa de Estudillo' (way/158967014): middle (67 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3364381: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Restored 19th-century Mexican and early American town.

text.description:
Old Town San Diego State Historic Park is a collection of preserved and rebuilt buildings from 1820 to 1870, when this was the heart of San Diego. Five of the buildings are original adobes, and there are also a schoolhouse, a blacksmith shop, a newspaper office and a stable with carriages. The park was established in 1968.

For a phone photographer, the best single frame is in the courtyard of Casa de Estudillo, a house built in 1827 and a National Historic Landmark in its own right. Whitewashed adobe walls, wooden verandas and the open courtyard fit neatly into one picture, and the park's older buildings sit behind. Walk in, turn to face the adobe walls and you have the scene without crowds of shopfronts around it.

If you have time for a second picture, La Plaza de Las Armas is also in the park. The tall flagpole in the middle, the old buildings and the visitors passing through make a lively street-life shot. Heritage Park is a separate place with a row of pastel-trimmed Victorian houses with porches, a very different look from the adobe.

Aim for early morning. Guides say the park gets busy by midday at weekends and that many shops open late, so the courtyard is calmer first thing. Take a slow look around before you shoot, because the walls, doorways and veranda posts all make good simple details as well as the wide view.
text.geographic_location: The park is in the Old Town neighbourhood of San Diego, at the foot of Presidio Hill and right next to Presidio Park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Old Town neighbourhood of San Diego. The park's mapped centre is to the north-west of it, about 1 minute on foot. The courtyard of Casa de Estudillo is the recommended viewpoint nearby, so once inside the park, look for it and use it as your subject. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the walls, veranda and courtyard together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as doorways, beams and whitewashed corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Casa de Estudillo (inside the courtyard, facing the adobe walls). Whitewashed adobe walls, wooden verandas and a courtyard framed by the historic house, with the park's older architecture in the background. The view to aim for is whitewashed adobe, wooden verandas and the courtyard framed by the house, with the park's older buildings behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the wall with a lower grid line so the verandas stay level. Keep a veranda post or doorway at one edge to add depth. If you want something different, the flagpole in La Plaza de Las Armas is a good alternative subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the whitewashed wall to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the white keeps its texture and the shaded verandas stay readable. Keep the phone level to stop the walls leaning.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the weekend crowds arrive and while the shops are still shut.

text.access_note: The park is a public state historic park, and there is no charge to enter the park or its museums, but check the official site before you go for tours and opening times.

name: Seaport Village
label: Seaport Village
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Embarcadero Marina Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Embarcadero Marina Park' (way/30929735): middle (465 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31240713: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Seaport Village' (423 m across).
notes: Waterfront shopping village with bay views.

text.description:
Seaport Village is a waterfront shopping and dining complex on San Diego Bay, made up of low buildings in different styles, from Victorian to traditional Mexican, linked by winding walkways instead of streets. It was built on landfill and opened in 1980. It holds more than 70 shops, galleries and eateries, and it has a working carousel with hand-carved animals, built in 1895. That mix of colourful frontages, paths and water makes it easy to photograph, and almost everything is at walking pace, so you can stop and shoot as you wander.

The best overall picture is the wide harbour view from Embarcadero Marina Park, on the yacht basin edge beside the village. From there you look across the boats towards the Grand Hyatt and Marriott towers, with part of the downtown skyline above the masts. Once you are in the village, the carousel is the other strong subject: the string lights, shops and paths surround it, with the bay behind. Take one wide shot of the marina first, then walk in for closer shots of the carousel and the shopfronts. Keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines, and look for a foreground, such as a boat or a railing, to give the picture depth. The carousel's status can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Seaport Village is on the downtown waterfront of San Diego, on the edge of San Diego Bay. It is within walking distance of the San Diego Convention Center and the cruise ship terminal.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from downtown San Diego, near the Convention Center or the cruise ship terminal, and head to the bay edge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the marina and skyline view, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the carousel and shopfronts. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tower tops or a single boat.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Embarcadero Marina Park (yacht basin edge beside Seaport Village). A wide view across the marina and yacht basin, with the Grand Hyatt and Marriott towers rising above the boats. From here you look across the marina and yacht basin, with the Grand Hyatt and Marriott towers rising above the boats. The village itself lies to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on a lower line, with the towers filling the upper part of the picture. Include a few boats in the foreground for depth. For a different shot, walk into the village and frame the Seaport Village Carousel with its string lights and the bay behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. A Live Photo can catch the carousel moving; hold the phone steady against your body or a railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually suits the marina view and brings out the village's string lights. Mornings are generally quieter for clear shots of the paths.

text.access_note: Seaport Village is an open pedestrian complex that you can walk around, but individual shops, rides and attractions may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: San Diego–Coronado Bridge
label: Coronado Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Coronado Tidelands Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Coronado Tidelands Park' (way/44501074): edge nearest the subject (728 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Curving blue bridge across San Diego Bay.

text.description: The San Diego–Coronado Bridge is the long, sweeping curve that carries traffic across San Diego Bay between downtown San Diego and Coronado. It opened on 3 August 1969, during the celebrations for San Diego's 200th anniversary. It is about 3.4 km (2.1 miles) long. Its curve is there for a practical reason: the Navy wanted at least 61 m (200 feet) of clearance for ships, and bending the route let the road climb gently enough to reach that height. That curve is also what makes it so good to photograph. From the Coronado bayfront you can line it up against the downtown skyline, with the roadway arching overhead and the water in front. The bridge is also known for the big murals on its eastern support pillars, part of Chicano Park. Chicano Park is a second good place to photograph if you want colour and texture rather than a skyline. Walking is not allowed on the bridge itself, so every good view is from the shoreline or below. Start at Coronado Tidelands Park and walk the bayfront path to find the angle you like. Look for the gap where the curve of the bridge sits above the buildings. Keep your phone level so the skyline does not lean. If you have time, try Cesar Chavez Park Public Pier 16 for a view of the whole arc running out over the water toward Coronado.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses San Diego Bay between downtown San Diego and Coronado. Its eastern end meets Interstate 5 just south-east of downtown.
text.directions_text: Use the map to reach Coronado Tidelands Park on the Coronado bayfront. Follow the bayfront path rather than trying to walk on the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the bridge's curve and the skyline in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the city buildings under the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Coronado Tidelands Park (Coronado side, bayfront promenade under the east end of the bridge). The downtown San Diego skyline with the bridge's curve arching overhead, usually framed head-on across the bay. From here the photo shows the downtown San Diego skyline with the bridge's curve arching overhead, usually framed head-on across the bay. On the map the bridge is to the south-east of this point. If the view is crowded or blocked, Cesar Chavez Park Public Pier 16 shows the full arc of the bridge with downtown behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the skyline up with a horizontal grid line so the horizon stays level. Put the water in the lower third and let the bridge's curve sweep across the top. For a different view, Chicano Park frames the support pillars against the murals.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At blue hour, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise gives soft side-light and a near-empty park. Blue hour is best for the bridge and the city lights.

text.access_note: Coronado Tidelands Park is a public park, but the bridge itself is not open to pedestrians or cyclists, and drone rules apply near it, so check the current rules and that the pier and park are open before you go.

name: Cabrillo National Monument
label: Cabrillo Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Old Point Loma Lighthouse' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Old Point Loma Lighthouse' (way/90687227): middle (16 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6173923: large area 'Cabrillo National Monument' (1576 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Statue of Cabrillo with views over the bay and skyline.

text.description: Cabrillo National Monument sits at the southern tip of the Point Loma peninsula and marks Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo's landing at San Diego Bay on 28 September 1542, the first time a European expedition set foot on what later became the US West Coast. For photographs, the best-known subject is the Old Point Loma Lighthouse, a whitewashed tower with a black lantern room, standing on the highest point in the park since 1855. It was closed in 1891 because fog and low cloud often hid the light, which stood 129 metres (422 feet) above sea level. Today that same height gives wide views over the harbour, the downtown skyline and Coronado. For the lighthouse itself, the recommended viewpoint is its east-facing entrance side, where the white walls stand out against sky or ocean. A cypress nearby can help frame the shot. For a second picture, walk to the Cabrillo statue overlook, where the skyline, San Diego Bay and Coronado sit across the water. The statue is a limestone replica, 1988, of the 1949 sandstone original, which weathered badly. If the tide is low, the tide pools offer a quieter, more textured foreground with the Pacific beyond. The Whale Overlook, south of the lighthouse, is worth a look from December to March. Allow time to wander, as the best angles are a short walk apart.
text.geographic_location: At the southern tip of the Point Loma peninsula in San Diego, looking across San Diego Bay to Coronado and the downtown skyline. The monument takes in the old lighthouse, the visitor centre and former coastal defences.
text.directions_text: Head for the southern tip of the Point Loma peninsula, the far end of the peninsula from central San Diego. No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Once in the monument, make for the Old Point Loma Lighthouse, the highest point in the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole lighthouse against the sky. Use the default lens (1x) for the overlook views of the skyline and bay. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Coronado, boats on the bay or details of the lantern room.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Old Point Loma Lighthouse (east-facing entrance side, for morning light). The whitewashed 1855 lighthouse with its black lantern room, framed against the ocean or sky, sometimes with a cypress for framing. For the lighthouse, stand on its east-facing entrance side. From there the whitewashed 1855 lighthouse, with its black lantern room, can fill the frame against the ocean or sky, and a cypress can sit to one side as a natural frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the tower upright against them. Crouch a little and tilt the phone up as little as you can, so the walls don't lean in. Include a bit of sky above the lantern room. For a different picture, try the Cabrillo statue overlook, where the skyline, bay and Coronado stretch across the water, or the tide pools for a foreground of rock ledges and pools.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the lighthouse wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white walls keep their detail against a bright sky. Use panorama at the overlook for the sweep of bay and skyline, moving slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light suits the lighthouse's east-facing entrance side. Fog and low cloud can drift in, so check the sky before you set out.

text.access_note: This is a national park site: check the official site before you go for entry, opening arrangements and what is open inside the lighthouse and visitor areas.

name: Santa Fe Depot
label: Santa Fe Depot
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Broadway' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Kettner Boulevard and Broadway (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6108409728: the OpenStreetMap point 'San Diego'.

text.description:
Santa Fe Depot is San Diego's grand railway station, built in the Spanish Colonial Revival style and best known for its twin domes. It opened on 8 March 1915, in time for the Panama–California Exposition, and replaced a small red-and-green Victorian depot from 1887. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is a San Diego Historic Landmark. It is still a working station, with Amtrak, Coaster trains, the San Diego Trolley and buses all passing through, so there is usually something happening in the frame.

The building photographs well because its shapes are strong and simple: arches, domes and a long façade with plenty of detail. From the street corner on Broadway, by the fountain in front of the depot, you get a lower, street-level view of the building with the fountain beside you. A photo of the station under construction in 1914 is described as having been taken from around this corner, so a similar angle gives your picture a pleasantly old-fashioned look.

For a second view, walk into the forecourt. Facing the front, you can frame the domes and arches with the tiled ground and fountain in the foreground. Or go to America Plaza and shoot the depot alongside the red trolley station, with trains and trolleys passing through the frame. Stay clear of doorways and platforms so you don't block passengers.
text.geographic_location: The depot stands in the Core district of downtown San Diego, with its fountain at the Broadway corner in front of the building.
text.directions_text: The depot is in the Core district of downtown San Diego. From elsewhere in the city, arrive by train, Trolley or bus, since the station is a transport hub, and head to the Broadway corner by the fountain. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the façade and fountain together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building will not fit from the corner, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the domes and tile detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Kettner Boulevard and Broadway (corner by the fountain in front of the depot). The depot's façade and fountain seen from the street corner at the edge of the forecourt, which is a more street-level angle on the building. Stand on Broadway, at the corner by the fountain in front of the depot. This is a street-level view from the edge of the forecourt, so you look at the building across the open space rather than from right in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the building straight so it doesn't lean. Place the fountain low in the frame as a foreground and let the domes and arches fill the upper part. If you want a different view, the forecourt gives a straight-on shot of the twin domes with the tiled ground in front, and America Plaza lets you include the red trolley station and moving trains.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the building's lit wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky stays blue and the walls keep their detail. Try a Live Photo when a trolley or train moves through the background, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the plaster and tiles. Moving trains and trolleys are part of the scene at any hour.

text.access_note: The forecourt and street corner are open public space, but this is a working station, so check the official site before you go for any access changes or building work.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters light-coloured plaster and tiles.
The forecourt and Broadway corner are generally open to the public.

name: Botanical Building
label: Botanical Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lily Pond' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lily Pond' (way/701452865): middle (89 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM W25775425 (Botanical Building): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Lath-house conservatory with a lily pond.

text.description:
The Botanical Building sits on El Prado in Balboa Park, and the best-known photo of it is taken across the Lily Pond. From the pond's edge on the El Prado side you look over the water at the building. Its lath walls and roofline are mirrored in the surface, with lilies and lotus floating in the foreground. Guides often call this the most photographed scene in Balboa Park, and it is easy to see why: the pond gives you a natural frame and a ready-made foreground.

The reflection is at its best on calm days, so a still morning gives you the cleanest result. Early morning and golden hour are the favoured times. Crouch slightly or stand right at the edge so the plants sit low in the frame and the building fills the water behind them.

If you go inside, expect light filtering through the slatted roof onto tree ferns, orchids and palms, with the lath ceiling behind. Check the official site before you go to see whether the building has finished its renovation and reopened. Ask on arrival or check the same site for any rules on interior photography. The pond view itself is outdoors on El Prado, at 1549 El Prado, and costs nothing to enjoy.
text.geographic_location: In Balboa Park, San Diego, on El Prado beside the Lily Pond.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Balboa Park and El Prado (1549 El Prado). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building and its reflection together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are right at the water's edge and want more lilies in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the lath roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the pond's edge on the El Prado side, facing the building across the water). The Botanical Building's lath walls and roofline mirrored in the water, with lilies and lotus in the foreground. Face north across the water to the Botanical Building. The lath walls and roofline mirror in the pond, with lilies and lotus in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the water's surface near the middle of the frame, so the building and its reflection get equal space. Keep a few lilies or lotus leaves low in the shot for depth. Inside, if photography is allowed, aim up at the slatted roof and let the ferns and palms fill the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the reflection stays rich. Wait for ripples to settle, or take a Live Photo and pick the stillest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or golden hour on a calm day, when the reflection is strongest.

text.access_note: The Lily Pond view is open outdoors on El Prado, but check the official site before you go, both for the building's opening status and for interior photography rules.

name: California Tower
label: California Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Panama' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Panama' (relation/17826594): middle (161 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/936855343: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'California Quadrangle' (56 m across).
notes: Baroque tower and landmark of Balboa Park.

text.description:
California Tower is the tall, slender landmark near the main entrance to Balboa Park, at the Cabrillo Bridge end of El Prado, rising beside the blue-and-gold dome of the California Building. It was built for the 1915–16 Panama–California Exposition and designed by Bertram Goodhue. Its look is Spanish, with Mexican-style details and colour. It stands 198 feet (60 m) tall, and its three tiers change shape from a square to an octagon to a circle, which gives it a pleasing outline against the sky. The buildings now house the Museum of Us, and the carillon in the tower chimes every quarter-hour.

From there you look west along El Prado, with the tower to the left of the avenue and the exposition-era buildings framing the shot. Historic photographers used this plaza too, and a 1915 postcard view was taken from the same spot. The tower is a short walk away, so it will look fairly small at first. Let the long arcaded buildings on either side lead the eye towards it, and keep the tower upright by lining it up with the gridlines. If you want a different angle, try Cabrillo Bridge, which gives a long, straight approach with the tower and dome at the far end. Alcázar Garden is another option, with the tower rising behind the hedges, arches and tiled fountains.
text.geographic_location: In Balboa Park, San Diego, at the Cabrillo Bridge end of El Prado, where the bridge brings you into the park. The tower is part of the California Quadrangle, which now houses the Museum of Us.
text.directions_text: Enter the park over Cabrillo Bridge, which leads to the California Quadrangle. From there the tower is about 3 minutes on foot to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole of El Prado with the tower on the left. Then try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower and dome closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and buildings, and keep the tower away from the edge of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Panama (west side of the plaza, looking west along El Prado). The tower stands to the left of El Prado, framed by the plaza and the surrounding exposition-era buildings. The tower sits to the left of the avenue, framed by the plaza and the exposition-era buildings. This is the standard angle on the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the tower on a vertical line so it stays straight. Keep the phone level and use the arcades and building edges along El Prado as lines leading towards it. For a different view, Cabrillo Bridge shows the tower and dome at the end of a long approach, and Alcázar Garden shows the tower behind hedges, arches and tiled fountains.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower or dome to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays blue and the details of the stonework and dome are not washed out. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, as the tower is a narrow subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is usually a good bet, because the sun is behind you as you look west and lights the front of the buildings. Late afternoon puts the sun more in front of you, so you may need to lower the exposure slider or step to one side.

text.access_note: The tower's guided climb is paid, so check the official site for museum details and current access before you go.

name: Old Point Loma Lighthouse
label: Point Loma Lighthouse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Old Point Loma Lighthouse' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/90687227: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old Point Loma Lighthouse' (16 m across).
notes: 1855 lighthouse on the Point Loma headland.

text.description:
Old Point Loma Lighthouse is a whitewashed tower with a black lantern room, standing near the top of the Point Loma peninsula where San Diego Bay meets the Pacific. It was built by the United States government in 1855 and first lit at sunset on 15 November that year. It sits within Cabrillo National Monument and is now a museum rather than a working light. The simple white shape, the black lantern and the keeper's house beside it make a tidy, friendly subject, and the bay and open sky behind give you a clean background.

The light only shone until 1891. Because it stood on a cliff about 400 feet up, fog and low cloud often hid it from ships, so a lower lighthouse replaced it. In 1984 the National Park Service re-lit it for a celebration, the first time in 93 years.

A paved path circles the building, so you can choose your side to suit the hour. The east-facing entrance side is the classic view, with the lantern room against clear sky, and morning light is said to be cleanest there. In the afternoon the white picket fence casts pleasing shadows. For a wider, quieter view from a distance, try the Kelp Forest Overlook, which looks back at the lighthouse with the ocean beyond. Wind can be strong on the headland, so hold your phone with both hands.
text.geographic_location: Old Point Loma Lighthouse is on the Point Loma peninsula at the mouth of San Diego Bay, inside Cabrillo National Monument in San Diego, California.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed near here, so start from the Point Loma area of San Diego and go by taxi or hired scooter to Cabrillo National Monument. The lighthouse stands near the top of the headland, and a paved path circles it. Once you are on the path, follow it round to the east-facing entrance side and use the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lighthouse with the keeper's house and sky around it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the grounds and fence in the frame, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the black lantern room against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. To get the tower in frame, step back a few metres on the east-facing entrance side of the paved path that circles the building. From there the whitewashed tower and its black lantern room fill the view, framed by the grounds and the keeper's house, with the bay and sky behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, keeping it upright by lining it up with the grid. Include a little of the keeper's house or the picket fence to give a sense of scale. For a quieter, wider alternative, the Kelp Forest Overlook gives a distant view of the lighthouse with the ocean beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls keep their detail and the sky stays blue. Take a few frames from different spots along the path, as the light changes the look of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid-morning or morning for the front (east) side; afternoon if you want the shadows of the white picket fence.

text.access_note: The lighthouse grounds sit within Cabrillo National Monument, which has an entry fee, so check the official site before you go for current access and rules, including any for photographing inside.

name: Spreckels Organ Pavilion
label: Spreckels Organ
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Panama' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Panama' (relation/17826594): middle (161 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31240523: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Spreckels Organ Pavillion' (91 m across).
notes: Open-air pavilion with a giant pipe organ.

text.description: The Spreckels Organ Pavilion is a semicircular, Italian-Renaissance-style outdoor stage in Balboa Park, built for the 1915 Panama–California Exposition. It holds the Spreckels Organ, which has more than 5,000 pipes and is described as the world's largest pipe organ in a fully outdoor venue. John D. Spreckels and his brother Adolph gave the pavilion and organ to the people of San Diego on 31 December 1914. It photographs well because the curved colonnade and the tiered seating make a calm, symmetrical shape that fits neatly into a phone frame. From the north side of Plaza de Panama you look south along the long approach, and the whole structure sits framed at the end with the organ building behind it. That gives you the classic wide view without needing to get close. If you walk down to the pavilion itself, a wide view of the front facade works well with people strolling in the foreground. You can also try close, layered shots of the pillars, arches and gables. Free organ concerts take place on Sunday afternoons at 2 pm, and the crowds can block the front view, so a quieter day is easier for a clean shot. Trams and low-flying planes can be noisy overhead, which matters more if you are recording video or Live Photos. Confirm the exact spot for the wide view when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: In Balboa Park, San Diego, at the corner of President's Way and Pan American Road East, just south of Plaza de Panama on the Prado side of the park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The official address for the nearby parking area is 2125 Pan American Road East, and the pavilion is at 1549 El Prado. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole colonnade framed down the approach. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move close and want the full curve of the facade. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the arches and gables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Panama (north side of the square, looking south toward the pavilion). The pavilion's curved colonnade and tiered seating framed at the end of the long Esplanade approach, with the organ building in the distance. From here the curved colonnade and tiered seating are framed at the end of the long Esplanade approach, with the organ building in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the centre of the colonnade with the middle of the frame so the symmetry holds. Keep some path or paving in the foreground to lead the eye towards the pavilion. For a different view, walk down to the front of the pavilion for a wide shot of the whole facade with people in the foreground. Or move in close for layered shots of pillars and arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the colonnade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Use the ultra-wide only when you are close, as it stretches the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a quieter moment rather than Sunday around the 2 pm concert, when crowds can block the front view. Late-afternoon light can look good falling through the archways, though that tip may not hold at every time of year.

text.access_note: The pavilion is an open-air venue in a public park, but events may change what you can access, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Trams and low-flying planes can be loud near the pavilion, which can spoil video or Live Photos.
Late-afternoon light falling through the archways can look good, but it may not hold at every time of year.
Crowds at the Sunday concert can block the front view of the pavilion.
The exact spot on the north side of Plaza de Panama should be confirmed on arrival.

name: Ocean Beach Pier
label: Ocean Beach Pier
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ocean Beach Tidepools' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Long fishing pier, popular for sunsets.

text.description: Ocean Beach Pier is the landmark of Ocean Beach, the laid-back beach neighbourhood where San Diego meets the Pacific at the mouth of the San Diego River. The pier has been closed to the public since storm damage, and the City of San Diego is keeping it closed while it plans a long-term replacement. That means the best photos are taken from the shore, not from the pier itself. Walk to the tidepools at the foot of Newport Avenue, below the pier, and shoot from there. From there you get a low, close view of the pier's underside and its supports, with rocks, sea life and birds in the foreground. Pelicans and gulls make good subjects. If you want the classic view instead, step back to the shore end and photograph the concrete approach and gate, with the ocean and surf stretching out beyond. Ocean Beach has been called by that name since 1887, and surfing was introduced to San Diego here in 1916, so a surfer in the frame suits the place. Go at low tide, when the tidepool area is at its best. Because the pier's status can change, check the current situation before you set out.
text.geographic_location: Ocean Beach Pier is in the Ocean Beach neighbourhood of San Diego, on the Pacific coast about 7 miles (11 km) north-west of downtown. It sits south of Mission Bay and directly north of Point Loma, at the foot of Newport Avenue.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Head for the Ocean Beach neighbourhood, about 7 miles (11 km) north-west of downtown San Diego. Then make your way to the foot of Newport Avenue, where the Ocean Beach Tidepools are, below the pier. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the close, low view of the pier's supports. Use the default lens (1x) for the pier and surf from the shore end. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for pelicans and gulls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk to the Ocean Beach Tidepools at the foot of Newport Avenue, beneath the pier, and stand there. From here the photo shows the underside and supports of the pier, with sea life and birds in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone low, close to the rocks, and let the pier's supports lead the eye out to sea. Switch on the gridlines to keep the horizon level. For an alternative, photograph the pier's concrete approach and gate from the shore end, with the ocean and surf beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pier or the nearest rock to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. For birds, use telephoto and take a burst or a Live Photo, so you can pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Low tide, when the tidepool area is at its best. Check the tide times for the day before you go.

text.access_note: The pier itself is closed to the public, so check the official City of San Diego site for the current status before you go; the tidepool area at the foot of Newport Avenue is the place to photograph from.
claims_not_in_sources: The rocks at the tidepools can be wet and slippery, so care is needed when walking and holding a phone low.
Pelicans and gulls are often found around the pier area.
The coast faces west, so the sun sets over the sea and the pier can look good in evening light.

name: Cabrillo Bridge
label: Cabrillo Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cabrillo Bridge' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cabrillo Canyon Bridge' (way/107643088): middle (57 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1672334: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cabrillo Bridge' (260 m across).
notes: Arched bridge forming the western entrance to Balboa Park.

text.description: Cabrillo Bridge is the grand western approach to Balboa Park, carrying El Prado across Cabrillo Canyon towards the museums. It was built for the Panama–California Exposition of 1915 and was the first multiple-arched cantilever bridge in California. It has seven arches on fourteen hollow concrete pillars, and the main span stands 120 feet (37 m) above the canyon floor. The whole structure, including approaches, is about 279 m long. That scale makes it a good phone subject. Use that point for a longer view towards the bridge, and zoom in to pick out the arches and deck. As a separate, approximate alternative, the centre of the span looks out over the deck and railings to the Downtown San Diego skyline and the gardens and buildings of Balboa Park, with the highway passing far below. From there, keep the railings or the line of the deck in the frame so the picture has depth, and tap the skyline to set focus. The footway is shared with a two-lane road, so keep your feet on the pavement and out of traffic when you step back for a shot. The deck is busiest at weekends and during events, so early morning is calmer, and sunset gives a warm glow over the city and bridge. For another view, Nate's Point Dog Park shows the arches from below, with the California Tower beyond the east end. It involves unpaved trails with some descent.
text.geographic_location: On the western edge of Balboa Park, in the uptown part of San Diego, where El Prado crosses Cabrillo Canyon. State Route 163 runs along the canyon floor beneath it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, and the bridge can be reached on foot. The bridge carries El Prado over the canyon, close to Sixth Avenue, which forms the park's western boundary. If you want the alternative view, continue to the bridge and walk out along the footway to the middle of the span. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the bridge to the south, then use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and the deck. If you walk out to the middle of the span, the ultra-wide (0.5x) takes in the deck, the railings and the skyline together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Cabrillo Bridge (center of the span, looking out over the deck). Downtown San Diego skyline and Balboa Park's gardens and buildings beyond the bridge's railings, with the highway passing below. As an approximate alternative, stand at the centre of the span on Cabrillo Bridge and look out over the deck, with the Downtown San Diego skyline and Balboa Park's gardens and buildings beyond the railings and the highway passing below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines. From where you stand, place the bridge along a lower third and let the sky fill the rest of the frame. If you go to the centre of the span, place the line of the railing along a lower third with the skyline above it, and stand slightly to one side of the footway so the deck leads the eye into the picture. For another view, Nate's Point Dog Park gives a view of the arches from underneath.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge or skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little at sunset so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset gives a golden glow over the city and the bridge. Early morning is less crowded, and weekends and event days are busiest.

text.access_note: The bridge is a public road with a footway, but it has been closed for works before, so check the official site before you go.
